Yes, it is spontaneous at 25 °C because ΔG° is negative. (If your ΔG was positive, conclude “not spontaneous” for the mark.)

(i) ΔH is positive — endothermic (products higher than reactants). The bonds in the reactants are stronger than those in the products (more energy absorbed breaking bonds than released forming them).

(ii) ΔG° is negative because the reaction is spontaneous. ΔS° must be positive: since ΔH° > 0, only a positive ΔS° can make ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° negative. The products are more disordered than the reactants.

(iii) Mix known volumes of the two solutions (one of known concentration, the other in equal or excess amount), both at the same starting temperature, in an insulated vessel (polystyrene cup with lid); stir and record the temperature change (lowest temperature). q = m c ΔT (m = mass of solution, c = 4.18 J g−1 K−1); n(limiting reactant) = cV; ΔH = +q/n in kJ mol−1.

(iv) Heat gained from the surroundings (container not well insulated) makes ΔT too small; incomplete reaction. Minimise by insulating the container (lid, polystyrene) or extrapolating a temperature–time graph.

(v) As T increases, TΔS° becomes larger so ΔG° becomes more negative → more spontaneous. As T decreases, TΔS° gets smaller so ΔG° becomes less negative, and may become positive when ΔH° > TΔS° → non-spontaneous at low T.

(ii) ΔS° = [4(189) + 150] − 305 = +601 J K−1 mol−1 (0.601 kJ K−1). Positive: products are more disordered (4 mol of gas are formed from a solid).

(i) ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. ΔS is negative (liquid → solid), so −TΔS is positive and grows as T increases. ΔG becomes less negative/more positive, so freezing becomes less spontaneous (above a certain T the reverse, melting, is favoured).

(ii) At ΔG = 0, T = ΔH/ΔS = (−9830 J mol−1)/(−35.2 J K−1 mol−1) = 279 K = 6 °C (convert kJ to J first). This is the melting/freezing point: solid and liquid benzene are in equilibrium; below it freezing is spontaneous, above it melting is.

At high T, the −TΔS° term is large and negative, outweighing positive ΔH°, so ΔG° < 0 → spontaneous [2].

At low T, TΔS° is smaller than ΔH°, so ΔG° > 0 → not spontaneous [1].

A spontaneous reaction is one that occurs without continuous input of energy from outside (once any activation barrier is overcome). It releases Gibbs energy that could do work, so ΔG is negative. It does not mean “fast”.

(i) H2(g) is an element in its standard state. By definition, its formation from itself involves no change, so ΔHf = 0.

(ii) C3H6 + H2 → C3H8: ΔH = −104 − (+20.4) = −124.4 kJ mol−1.

(iii) ΔS = 270 − (267 + 131) = −128 J K−1 mol−1. It is negative because 2 mol of gas become 1 mol.

(iv) ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −124.4 − 298 × (−0.128) = −86.3 kJ mol−1 (units needed).

(v) The reaction stops being spontaneous when ΔG = 0, i.e. T = ΔH/ΔS = −124.4 ÷ −0.128 = 972 K (699 °C). Above this, the decomposition of propane is spontaneous.
